findings.description: The customer search handler hides cards that do not match the name query but does not display an empty state when every card is hidden. The Customers markup contains the card grid and cards but no customer no-results message.

evidence.description: Search sets each card's hidden property based on the name query; there is no no-match branch.
The customer grid contains cards but no customer empty-state element.

findings.impact: A query with no matching names leaves the directory blank without guidance to revise or clear the search.
findings.recommendation: Show a no-matching-customers message when no cards match and provide a clear-search recovery action.
findings.title: Customer search can leave a blank directory when there are no matches

findings.description: Customer cards include buttons titled More actions, but the customer route registers no handler for them. The supplied source contains no menu behavior or feedback for these buttons.

evidence.description: Customer cards include icon buttons titled More actions.
The customer script handles search and invitations only; it does not wire card action buttons.

findings.impact: Users who try to access customer-specific actions reach a dead end.
findings.recommendation: Implement the customer action menu or clearly mark the buttons unavailable in the demo.
findings.title: Customer card “More actions” buttons have no action handler

findings.description: The Orders toolbar presents Export, Columns, Bulk actions, Saved filters, Date range, and Archive as buttons. The supplied Orders handler does not register behavior for these controls. The New order button does provide an explanatory demo toast, but the toolbar controls do not.

evidence.description: The page presents Export, Columns, Bulk actions, Saved filters, Date range, and Archive as buttons.
The handler registers search/status filtering, row viewing, dialog actions, and New order feedback, but not the toolbar controls.
New order has an explicit unavailable-in-demo toast.

findings.impact: Users can activate labeled controls without receiving an action or indication that the controls are unavailable.
findings.recommendation: Implement the labeled actions or identify them as unavailable in the demo with concise feedback, using the New order message as an existing pattern.
findings.title: Orders toolbar buttons have no implemented action or feedback

findings.description: The button is labeled Download, while its handler only displays “Report exported (demo only)” through the toast. The explicit demo-only wording reduces the risk of users interpreting this as a real export, but the supplied handler does not create or download a file.

evidence.description: The primary analytics action is labeled Download.
The click handler only shows an export toast with explicit demo-only wording.

findings.impact: The control's label implies a downloadable report, but activating it does not produce a file.
findings.recommendation: Provide a file download or relabel the control and message as a demo preview.
findings.title: Analytics Download control reports an export without creating a file

findings.description: Opening an order reveals a dialog marked aria-modal=true, but the handler does not move focus into the dialog, contain Tab navigation, close it on Escape, or restore focus to the View button. The shared Escape handler closes only the mobile menu.

evidence.description: The order overlay contains a dialog marked aria-modal=true and Close/Open record buttons.
The View handler reveals the dialog; close and confirm handlers hide it without moving or restoring focus.
Escape invokes setMenu(false); no dialog dismissal is handled there.

findings.impact: Keyboard focus can remain behind a dialog that claims to be modal, leaving users to navigate away from the dialog to reach its controls.
findings.recommendation: Move focus into the dialog when it opens, manage focus while it is open, close it on Escape, and return focus to the specific View button that opened it.
findings.title: Order details dialog does not manage keyboard focus or Escape dismissal

findings.description: The Dark mode switch is described as using darker surfaces at night. Its handler changes aria-checked and displays “Appearance preference updated,” but the supplied handler does not update a page theme. The stylesheet's aria-checked rule changes the switch itself.

evidence.description: The Dark mode switch is described as using darker surfaces at night.
The handler flips aria-checked and reports that the appearance preference was updated.
The aria-checked rule changes the switch track and thumb; the supplied styles contain no page-level theme rule.

findings.impact: Users receive confirmation that an appearance preference changed while the page surfaces remain unchanged.
findings.recommendation: Apply a page-level theme when the switch changes, or explain that the preference is unavailable in this demo and avoid success feedback that implies it was applied.
findings.title: Dark mode switch reports an update without applying a page theme

findings.description: The shared header renders the notification button with only an aria-hidden SVG child. The button has no text, aria-label, or title to identify its purpose.

evidence.description: The notification button has no text or naming attribute, and its only child SVG is aria-hidden.
The Analytics route repeats the unnamed notification button in its shared header.
The Customers route repeats the unnamed notification button in its shared header.
The Orders route repeats the unnamed notification button in its shared header.
The Settings route repeats the unnamed notification button in its shared header.
Activating the notification button currently produces an all-caught-up toast.

findings.impact: Screen-reader users may encounter an unnamed button and cannot identify the notification action before activating it.
findings.recommendation: Give the button a concise accessible name such as “Notifications.”
findings.title: The notification button has no accessible name

findings.description: The stylesheet sets outline:none on focus-visible navigation links and icon buttons. It also sets outline:0 on search inputs, with no focus treatment for the search box in the supplied styles. The navigation and icon controls appear across routes; search inputs appear on Customers and Orders.

evidence.description: The shared focus-visible rule removes outlines from navigation links and icon buttons.
The search input rule sets outline:0; no focus-within treatment is present in the supplied stylesheet.

findings.impact: Keyboard users may have difficulty identifying the currently focused navigation, header, or search control.
findings.recommendation: Replace the removed outlines with a visible focus treatment for links and icon buttons, and provide a focus treatment for the search input or its container.
findings.title: Focus outlines are removed from navigation and icon controls

findings.description: The Customers page presents All segments and Newest first as buttons. The customer script handles search and invitation feedback only; it does not change the cards or provide feedback for either button.

evidence.description: All segments and Newest first are presented as toolbar buttons.
The only registered customer-page handlers are for search input and the invite button.

findings.impact: Users cannot segment or sort the directory despite controls that suggest those operations are available.
findings.recommendation: Implement the segment and sort actions, or make their unavailable demo status clear.
findings.title: Customer segment and sort buttons are inert

findings.description: The slider ranges from 1 to 100,000 and its adjacent copy says it filters a summary metric. The handler displays 286 for every value up to 40,000 and 11 for every value above 40,000. This leaves the displayed count unchanged across most of the slider range and changes it only at one boundary.

evidence.description: The slider spans 1–100,000 and the adjacent copy describes filtering a summary metric.
The qualified-order count has only two fixed outcomes based on whether the slider value exceeds 40,000.

findings.impact: Users exploring the cutoff may interpret the displayed value as a calculated result even though it changes only at a single threshold.
findings.recommendation: Make the two-scenario behavior explicit or define a documented data model that updates the count across the slider range.
findings.title: Analytics cutoff changes the qualified-order count only at one threshold

findings.description: At widths up to 800px, the sidebar is moved off-screen with a transform. The menu handler changes the sidebar class and aria-expanded state but does not hide or disable the closed sidebar for keyboard navigation. Because the sidebar precedes the main content in the markup, its links can receive focus before the menu button while off-screen.

evidence.description: The mobile closed state applies transform:translateX(-100%); the open state reverses the transform.
Menu state toggles CSS classes and aria-expanded; it does not synchronize an inert or hidden state.
The sidebar and its navigation links occur before the main header containing the menu button.
The Orders route uses the same sidebar-before-header document order.

findings.impact: On mobile, keyboard focus can move through navigation links that are off-screen before reaching the visible menu button.
findings.recommendation: Remove the closed sidebar from sequential focus and the accessibility tree, and restore it when the menu opens. Keep aria-expanded synchronized with that state.
findings.title: Closed mobile navigation remains in the keyboard tab order

findings.description: On submit, the handler immediately sets the live status to “Saved successfully” and shows a success-like toast. If the alert threshold exceeds 80,000, it changes the live status to “Sync failed; your changes were not stored” after 450 ms. The toast remains visible for 3.2 seconds. The form copy explicitly describes this simulated success-then-failure sequence, and the final status clearly reports the failure; the supported concern is the brief overlapping feedback.

evidence.description: The form says values above $80,000 simulate a failed save after a successful acknowledgement; save status has aria-live=polite.
The submit handler announces success, shows a saved-preferences toast, and later sets failure status above the threshold.
Toast feedback stays visible for 3,200 ms unless replaced.

findings.impact: For the simulated failure case, the success-like toast remains visible after the live status changes to failure, so users receive overlapping outcome messages.
findings.recommendation: Keep the simulated success-then-failure behavior clear, but replace or dismiss the success toast when the failure status appears.
findings.title: Settings save briefly reports success before a simulated failure

findings.description: The Revenue performance panel presents a Last 6 months button, but the chart is static markup and the overview handler does not register behavior for the period control.

evidence.description: The Revenue performance panel includes a Last 6 months button.
The overview handler wires the mobile menu, notifications, and report-export demo control; it does not wire a chart period control.

findings.impact: Users cannot change the displayed chart period through a control that is presented as a button.
findings.recommendation: Implement period selection or present the current period as non-interactive text until alternate ranges are supported.
findings.title: Overview chart period button does not change the chart

findings.description: The settings submit handler reads the editable workspace name and interpolates it into a toast message. The shared toast helper assigns that message to `innerHTML`, so markup entered in the field is parsed when the toast is shown. The fixture has no backend or persistence path, which limits this to the current browser session, but the sink should not treat editable text as trusted HTML.

evidence.description: The workspace name is an editable form input.
The form value is interpolated into the toast message.
The shared toast helper inserts its argument with innerHTML.

findings.impact: A workspace name containing HTML can change the toast DOM and may execute event-handler markup in the page context.
findings.recommendation: Build the toast with DOM nodes and set the workspace name through textContent, or make the toast API accept text rather than arbitrary HTML.
findings.title: Workspace name is inserted into toast HTML

findings.description: Clicking the dark mode switch changes `aria-checked` and announces that the preference was updated, but the handler does not apply a theme class or theme attribute. The stylesheet only styles the switch state itself; no dark theme is selected by this interaction.

evidence.description: The switch is labeled Dark mode and described as changing workspace appearance.
The handler toggles the checked attribute and reports an updated preference.
The switch checked state changes the control styling; no theme application is present in the stylesheet rules.

findings.impact: The control reports a preference change while the workspace appearance remains unchanged.
findings.recommendation: Apply a theme state to the document when the switch changes, or adjust the control and feedback to describe a UI-only demo toggle.
findings.title: Dark mode switch changes its checked state without applying a theme

findings.description: `toast` writes `message` to `innerHTML`. A caller passes a value derived from editable value `team`; the inspected path contains no recognized HTML sanitizer.

evidence.description: HTML sink receives the traced value.
Call site supplies the value written to the HTML sink.
`team` is read from a DOM or browser-provided value.

findings.impact: Markup supplied through the editable value can be parsed as HTML in the current page context.
findings.recommendation: Render user-provided values with `textContent` or DOM nodes; if authored markup is required, sanitize it with a reviewed allowlist sanitizer.
findings.title: User-controlled content reaches an HTML rendering sink

findings.description: The analytics page says the order-value cutoff filters a summary metric, but the handler sets the qualified count to 286 for every cutoff at or below 40,000 and 11 above that. It does not filter an analytics dataset or derive the count from the orders fixture, so most slider positions change the displayed amount without meaningfully changing the count.

evidence.description: The slider is presented as a cutoff that filters the summary metric.
The qualified-order count is selected by a single fixed threshold.
The available order fixture is a separate fixed array; no analytics records are exported.

findings.impact: Users cannot explore how the qualified-order count changes across the slider range, and the displayed count is not traceable to route data.
findings.recommendation: Calculate the count from an analytics dataset that includes order values, or label the two outcomes as a deliberately simplified demo.
findings.title: Analytics cutoff count has only two hard-coded outcomes

findings.description: Opening the order preview only unhides the element marked `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`. The handler does not move focus into it, keep keyboard focus inside it, restore focus to the triggering row button on close, or close it on Escape. The shared Escape handler only closes the navigation menu.

evidence.description: The order preview is declared modal and contains close and confirm buttons.
The preview is opened by setting hidden to false; no focus management accompanies the operation.
The global Escape handler only updates the navigation menu state.

findings.impact: Keyboard and assistive-technology users may remain behind the modal or tab into background controls while it is marked modal.
findings.recommendation: Use a native dialog with an explicit open/close flow, or implement focus entry, focus containment, Escape dismissal, and focus restoration.
findings.title: Order dialog lacks a focus lifecycle

findings.description: The customer route embeds record values in its HTML cards, while `src/customers.js` imports the shared customer array but never reads it. Search filters the existing cards through their `data-customer` attributes. The current fixture values appear aligned, but updates to the array will not update the rendered customer directory.

evidence.description: The module imports the customer fixture and filters DOM cards without using the imported array.
Search logic acts on the pre-existing cards and their data attributes.
Customer names and profile values are embedded in static card markup.
A separate customer records array is exported from the shared fixture module.

findings.impact: Future edits can leave the shared fixture and visible directory out of sync, and the route currently pays to import unused data.
findings.recommendation: Choose one source for directory records: render cards from the imported fixture or remove the unused import and treat the HTML cards as canonical.
findings.title: Customer records have two separate source representations

findings.description: Submitting settings immediately writes “Saved successfully” and shows a success toast. For thresholds above 80,000, the handler changes the live status to a sync failure after 450 ms, while the toast remains visible for 3,200 ms. The route markup documents this simulation, but the success toast is not replaced when the failure state arrives.

evidence.description: Success feedback is issued before the delayed failure branch.
The status changes to a failure message only after the delay.
The toast remains visible until its independent timeout expires.

findings.impact: For the documented failure case, the user can receive success feedback and then see a failure status while the stale success toast remains.
findings.recommendation: Wait until the simulated result is known before announcing success, and show only the final outcome in both the status message and toast.
findings.title: Settings announces success before the simulated save can fail

findings.description: The settings stylesheet keeps `.fixed-field-row` at a 720 px minimum width. The mobile media rule changes the form row to one column but does not reset that minimum width, so the row can remain wider than the settings content at narrow viewports. This is inferred from CSS; no rendered viewport evidence was supplied.

evidence.description: The settings-specific form row has a fixed minimum width.
The mobile rule changes the form row grid but does not change its minimum width.
The workspace form uses the fixed-field-row class.

findings.impact: On narrow screens, form controls may extend beyond the content area and require horizontal page scrolling.
findings.recommendation: Remove the fixed minimum width at the mobile breakpoint and let the fields stack within the available content width.
findings.title: Settings form row retains a 720 px minimum width on mobile

findings.description: The shared table shell is configured for horizontal scrolling, but the orders-specific rule changes its overflow to visible while the table has a minimum width of 870 px. On narrower content areas, the table can extend beyond the shell instead of scrolling within it. This is a source-based layout conclusion; no viewport rendering was available.

evidence.description: The base table shell enables horizontal scrolling.
The orders override sets overflow visible and the table minimum width to 870 px.

findings.impact: At narrow widths, the table may widen the page and make neighboring content harder to reach without page-level horizontal scrolling.
findings.recommendation: Keep horizontal scrolling on the table shell while retaining the table minimum width, or provide another constrained overflow container.
findings.title: Orders table overflow override disables its horizontal scroll container

findings.description: The stylesheet explicitly removes the `:focus-visible` outline for navigation links and icon buttons without adding another focus indicator in that rule. This affects the shared sidebar links and icon controls, including the menu and notifications buttons.

evidence.description: The focus-visible rule sets outline to none for both selectors.
The shared header includes icon buttons and the sidebar contains navigation links.

findings.impact: Keyboard users may not be able to identify which of these controls currently has focus.
findings.recommendation: Provide a visible focus style for these selectors, such as an outline with adequate offset and contrast.
findings.title: Keyboard focus outlines are removed from navigation and icon buttons

findings.description: Rendered observation: at mobile width, the Workspace details card and fields continue beyond the screenshot’s right edge, cutting off text. At tablet width, the card also extends beyond the right edge. At desktop width, the form content extends into the area obscured by the Appearance and alerts card. Source observation: assets/styles.css:4 gives .fixed-field-row a 720px minimum width; the mobile rule at assets/styles.css:9 changes the form row’s column count but does not remove that minimum. The row is used by the workspace details form in settings/index.html:7. This source supports the overflow seen in the screenshots; no additional runtime behavior was inspected.

evidence.description: Rendered observation: at the supplied mobile viewport, the Workspace details card, fields, and helper copy are cut off at the right edge.
Rendered observation: the Workspace details card continues beyond the screenshot’s right edge, so its right boundary and surrounding canvas gutter are not visible.
Rendered observation: Workspace details form content reaches into the horizontal area covered by the Appearance and alerts card.
Source observation: assets/styles.css sets min-width:720px on .settings-page .fixed-field-row.
Source observation: assets/styles.css changes .settings-page .form-row to one column at the mobile breakpoint but leaves the fixed row minimum width in place.
Source observation: settings/index.html contains the fixed-field-row in the Workspace details form.

findings.impact: At mobile and tablet widths, part of the settings form is outside the visible page area. At desktop width, the form extends into the neighboring card’s area, weakening the separation between the two settings groups.
findings.recommendation: Remove the 720px minimum width from the settings form row and let its fields fit within the Workspace details panel. Keep the fields stacked at the mobile breakpoint, then confirm the form remains inside its card across the supplied widths.
findings.title: Workspace details form exceeds its available width

findings.description: Rendered observation: in the tablet screenshot, the trailing action column is beyond the captured right edge; in the mobile screenshot, the table is cut off partway through Channel, so the remaining fields are not initially visible. Source observation: `assets/styles.css:2` gives `.table-shell` horizontal overflow, but `assets/styles.css:4` overrides that for `.orders-page` with `overflow:visible` and sets the table minimum width to 870px. The supplied runtime inventory measures document widths of 891px at the 768px tablet viewport and 886px at the 390px mobile viewport. Inference: the route-specific override allows the wide table to contribute to page-level horizontal overflow instead of containing it in the table shell.

evidence.description: Rendered observation: the table extends beyond the viewport to the right of the Date column; its trailing action column is not in view.
Rendered observation: only the Order and Customer columns and the start of Channel are visible.

findings.impact: On narrow screens, users cannot see all order fields in the initial view, and the supplied measurements show the document wider than the viewport. Page-level horizontal overflow can make the rest of the interface harder to keep in view.
findings.recommendation: Restore horizontal scrolling on the orders table shell so the page stays within the viewport and the existing columns remain available by panning the table. This preserves the current table structure but still requires horizontal movement to reach off-screen fields; a compact mobile row layout would reduce panning at the cost of taller rows.

findings.description: Rendered observation: the “NS” letters in the desktop sidebar footer look faint against the mint avatar compared with the darker customer initials. Measurement supplied in the audit inventory: the computed foreground/background sample for `span.avatar` is 1.76:1 against a listed 4.5:1 threshold; this ratio was not independently recalculated, and its stated basis excludes transparency and compositing. Source corroboration: `assets/styles.css:2` sets a muted color on `.sidebar-footer span`, which also matches the footer avatar span.

evidence.description: The sidebar footer “NS” initials appear lighter than the customer initials. The 1.76:1 ratio is from the supplied computed-style sample, not a measurement of screenshot pixels.

findings.impact: The small workspace monogram is less legible than the customer initials, though the adjacent workspace name remains visible.
findings.recommendation: Set a darker foreground specifically for `.sidebar-footer .avatar`, leaving the workspace descriptor text muted.
findings.title: Sidebar footer initials are much lighter than customer initials

findings.description: Rendered observation: the supplied 390×844 screenshot shows the date, greeting, subtitle, paired actions, and first three KPI cards; the fourth card extends beyond the screenshot boundary. The trend and activity panels are not visible in the capture. Source observation: index.html:7 places the four metric cards before the later content panels, and assets/styles.css:9 sets both .grid-4 and .content-grid to one column at widths of 520px or less. Inference: a visitor seeking trend or activity context must scroll past the KPI stack. The screenshot does not show content being lost or clipped from the page; this is a product-priority tradeoff.

evidence.description: The first three cards are fully visible and the fourth is partly visible at the bottom of the 390×844 capture; no trend or activity panel appears within the captured viewport.

findings.impact: The captured first viewport exposes KPI values without trend or recent-activity context.
findings.recommendation: If quicker access to trends is a product priority on mobile, consider a denser KPI presentation. Keep labels and values easy to scan.
findings.title: The mobile first viewport is KPI focused

findings.description: Rendered observations: at mobile width, the revenue card is cut off at the right edge and the visible chart shows only Direct and Retail; the acquisition card also extends beyond the captured width. At tablet width, the chart card fills nearly all the visible analytics row and only the acquisition card's left edge appears at the far right. Source observations: `analytics/index.html:7` puts both cards in `.layout-2`; `assets/styles.css:2` defines `.layout-2` as two equal columns; `assets/styles.css:4` sets `.analytics-page .chart-frame` to a 680px minimum width; and `assets/styles.css:9` switches `.layout-2` to one column only at widths up to 520px. Inference: the chart's minimum width contributes to overflow at mobile, and the two-column row remains active at the 768px tablet viewport. The screenshots do not establish whether users can reveal the clipped content with horizontal scrolling.

evidence.description: The revenue card is clipped at the right edge, with only the Direct and Retail category labels visible; the acquisition card also continues beyond the capture width.
Only a narrow slice of the acquisition panel is visible at the far right of the analytics row.

findings.impact: Some chart categories and acquisition metrics fall outside the visible area at the supplied narrow viewports, making the analytics harder to scan and compare.
findings.recommendation: At narrow widths, reduce or remove the chart frame's 680px minimum width and stack the analytics cards by tablet width. If retaining the current chart scale is important for label spacing, contain horizontal scrolling within the chart area and make that scrolling evident; that option preserves chart size but requires users to scroll sideways.
findings.title: Analytics content extends beyond narrow viewports

findings.description: Rendered observation: the second card has noticeably squarer corners than the surrounding cards in the desktop, tablet, and mobile screenshots. specialist_assessments.assessment: Source observations: the five routes are separate HTML documents. Each loads the shared `src/app.js`, and four also load a route-specific module. The shared code is limited to helpers such as toast rendering; route markup and most displayed metrics are authored directly in each HTML file. Orders renders from the fixed `orders` array, while the customer route contains its cards in HTML and its module imports but does not use the `customers` array.
